target_name: Rancho Los Cerritos (Manuel Nieto grant remnant; Temple/Flint-Bixby ranch)
disclaimer: Hypothesis-neutral public-records screening. Nothing here asserts that any community is contaminated. The only soil fact anywhere is 'unstudied'. Geographic or temporal overlap does not establish exposure or causation. This is not medical advice and establishes no causation.
earliest_imagery: OLDEST TOPO: the Rancho Los Cerritos land is covered by the USGS Downey 30-minute quadrangle, 1:62,500, published 1896 (USGS Historical Topographic Map Collection; ScienceBase item 5a8a406be4b00f54eb3ed321, which returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch but is corroborated by its own catalog title and by Pastmaps' '1902 Map of Downey' / '1896 Downey' listings and the CSU Long Beach and LA Public Library historical-topo guides). The coastal-southern margin of the rancho is additionally covered by the older USGS Los Bolsas 1:62,500 sheet of 1886, which the Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands cultural-resources report cites as the earliest topo of its project area. OLDEST AERIAL: the earliest systematic aerial coverage verified for this landscape is a 1927 USDA frame held at UCSB (FrameFinder), explicitly reproduced as Figure D-1 in the Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands cultural-resources report; a 1928 USDA frame follows. (Fairchild/USDA flew the Los Angeles basin in 1927-1928, which is the standard EDR/Phase-I first aerial year for the LA basin.) Net: oldest topo = 1886 (Los Bolsas, coastal margin) / 1896 (Downey, inland footprint); oldest confirmed aerial = 1927.
review_gap_note: HEADLINE FIGURE. review_gap_years = 1927 (the earliest aerial photograph the on-footprint CEQA historical review actually examined) minus ~1912 (the approximate close of the arsenical cattle-tick-eradication dipping era) = 15 years of that dipping window sitting BELOW the review's imagery floor. The headline document is the Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands Restoration Project, Draft IS/MND Appendix F (Cultural Resources Assessment), dated 2023-04-10, which explicitly reproduces and discusses USDA aerials of 1927, 1928, 1938, 1952, 1962, 1965, 1974, 1994 and 2001 (Appendix D, Figures D-1 through D-9) and USGS topos of 1886 Los Bolsas, 1896 Downey, 1935 Los Alamitos, 1941 Las Bolsas, 1942 Downey, 1974 Los Alamitos (Appendix G). A parallel on-footprint document, the City of Long Beach 'Los Cerritos Wetlands Oil Consolidation and Restoration Project' EIR cultural-resources section, examined aerials 1928, 1947, 1953, 1963 and 1972 (floor 1928, gap = 16). IMPORTANT QUALIFIER 1: these are cultural-resources/archaeological CEQA reviews, not hazardous-materials Phase I ESAs; a small dip facility being 'below the floor' is an expected data-availability limitation, not a hazard finding. QUALIFIER 2 (target-specific): the dipping activity actually documented for THIS ranch is SHEEP dipping during the Bixby period (roughly 1866-1890), which ended ~1890 with subdivision -- EARLIER than the ~1912 cattle-tick reference date. Measured against the sheep-dipping era's close (~1890) the unreviewed window widens to 1927-1890 = ~37 years, so 15 is the conservative mechanical figure. QUALIFIER 3 (geography): the two wetlands documents sit at the coastal-southern margin (mouth of the San Gabriel River) where the historic Rancho Los Cerritos boundary abuts Rancho Los Alamitos; their land narratives are largely Los Alamitos/Hellman, so they index the review floor for this landscape rather than the inland Bixby Knolls/Lakewood/Bellflower core. No dedicated inland-footprint EIR enumerating its aerial floor was located in this pass; Lakewood (built 1950-1954 on former bean/beet fields) predates CEQA (1970) entirely and thus has no EIR.
dipping_records_summary: Unlike most targets in this program, dipping IS attested at this ranch by name -- but as SHEEP dipping, not a cattle-tick vat, and via an institutional museum rather than a newspaper or state-veterinarian record. The Rancho Los Cerritos Historic Site (a Long Beach city museum / National Historic Landmark) library exhibit 'The Bixby Sheep Ranching Period 1866-1890' states it 'features a photograph of the sheep being dipped in a chemical bath after shearing to prevent bug and parasite infestation.' This ties a dipping practice to the named ranch and to a specific era (up to ~30,000 sheep, sheared twice yearly, under Flint, Bixby & Co / Jotham Bixby 1866-1881). What the museum text does NOT provide: the chemistry of the bath (arsenical vs. lime-sulfur vs. tobacco/nicotine were all in period use), the physical location/coordinates of the dip, or whether it was a permanent vat or a portable/temporary bath. Newspaper-archive confirmation could not be obtained programmatically: the California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) returned HTTP 403 to automated queries this run, and Chronicling America was not successfully reached -- both are tooling access limits, not substantive negatives. Conclusion: a named-ranch sheep-dip is DOCUMENTED as a practice; a specific dip-vat structure with location and chemistry is NOT documented in the searchable materials. 'The searchable materials do not identify a located dip-vat' is distinct from 'no vat existed.'
sampling_frame_plausibility: Plausibility of an on-ranch working/dip facility is HIGH on terrain and operational grounds, and -- unusually for this program -- is reinforced by a named-ranch documentary attestation of dipping; but this remains a statement about physical plausibility and practice ONLY and asserts NOTHING about whether a persistent arsenical residue exists anywhere in soil today. Rancho Los Cerritos was a ~27,000-acre operation on the Los Angeles / San Gabriel River lowlands, exceptionally well watered (artesian conditions were strong enough that Bouton Lake formed from an 1895 well; the LA and San Gabriel Rivers and their distributary sloughs and wetlands cross the grant). Under Flint, Bixby & Co (1866-1890) it carried up to ~30,000 sheep sheared twice yearly -- exactly the flock size and management (post-shearing dip to control scab/keds/parasites) for which fixed dipping infrastructure was standard, and the museum confirms a dipping bath was in fact used. California enforced sheep-scab control by compulsory dipping in this era (California Statutes of 1900, secs. 597-599c, animallaw.info), and period sheep dips used tobacco/sulfur and, from the mid-19th century, arsenical formulations (e.g., Cooper's arsenic-sulfur dip, 1852). LIMITING CONSIDERATIONS: (a) the documented vector is sheep-scab dipping, whose chemistry was frequently lime-sulfur or nicotine rather than arsenic, so persistence is not assured even if a dip existed; (b) the dip's location within 27,000 acres is unknown and much of the grant is now dense post-1950 suburbia and channelized river, so any single historic dip point is a needle in a very large, heavily reworked haystack; (c) no imagery or record reviewed in this pass locates the facility on the ground.

findings.claim: HEADLINE: The on-footprint CEQA historical land-use review (Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands Restoration Project, Draft IS/MND Appendix F Cultural Resources, 2023-04-10) examined aerials only back to 1927 and USGS topos back to 1886/1896, leaving ~15 years of the pre-1912 arsenical-dipping era below its aerial floor (and ~37 years below it relative to this ranch's own sheep-dipping era, which ended ~1890).
findings.supporting: The report reproduces and discusses USDA aerials of 1927, 1928, 1938, 1952, 1962, 1965, 1974, 1994, 2001 (Appendix D, Figs D-1..D-9) and USGS topos 1886 Los Bolsas, 1896 Downey, 1935/1941/1942/1974 (Appendix G). Text: 'Based on the earliest known USDA aerial photographs of the Project area, in 1927...' 1927 minus ~1912 = 15-year unreviewed dipping window. The parallel Long Beach Los Cerritos Wetlands Oil Consolidation EIR used a 1928 floor (gap 16).
findings.counter_evidence: This is a cultural-resources/archaeological review, not a hazardous-materials Phase I ESA, so a dip below the imagery floor is an expected data-availability limitation, not a hazard. No dip facility is indicated in ANY reviewed year. Word-boundary searches of the full 243-page report returned zero hits for 'dipping', 'vat', or 'arsenic'. The document also sits at the coastal Los Alamitos/Hellman margin, not the inland Bixby-Knolls/Lakewood core, so it indexes the landscape's review floor rather than the exact Los Cerritos homestead.
findings.citation: Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands Restoration Project, Draft IS/MND, Appendix F Cultural Resources (2023-04-10), Appendices D and G; https://intoloscerritoswetlands.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/2023-04-10_SLCWRP-Draft-IS-MND_Appendix-F_Cultural.pdf . Grade A2.

findings.claim: Sheep dipping is DOCUMENTED at Rancho Los Cerritos by name: the site museum's 'Bixby Sheep Ranching Period 1866-1890' exhibit features a photograph of the ranch's sheep being dipped in a chemical bath after shearing to control parasites.
findings.supporting: Rancho Los Cerritos Historic Site (Long Beach city museum / National Historic Landmark), library-exhibit page: '...a photograph of the sheep being dipped in a chemical bath after shearing to prevent bug and parasite infestation.' Consistent with the ~30,000-head, twice-yearly-sheared Flint/Bixby sheep operation of 1866-1890.
findings.counter_evidence: The museum text gives NO chemistry (arsenical vs. lime-sulfur vs. tobacco/nicotine), NO location or coordinates, and does not establish a permanent vat vs. a portable/temporary bath. A documented dipping PRACTICE is not a located dip-vat STRUCTURE, and says nothing about any surviving soil residue. The dip photograph itself was not opened/verified in this pass; the attestation rests on the museum's exhibit description.
findings.citation: rancholoscerritos.org, 'Library Exhibit: The Bixby Sheep Ranching Period 1866-1890'; https://www.rancholoscerritos.org/library-exhibit-the-bixby-sheep-ranching-period-1866-1890/ . Grade B1 (institutional museum).

findings.claim: The oldest topographic maps covering the Rancho Los Cerritos land are the USGS Los Bolsas 1:62,500 sheet of 1886 (coastal margin) and the USGS Downey 1:62,500 sheet of 1896 (inland footprint).
findings.supporting: USGS Historical Topographic Map Collection lists a Downey CA 1:62,500 quad of 1896 (ScienceBase item 5a8a406be4b00f54eb3ed321); the Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands report cites '1886 Los Bolsas and 1896 Downey (both 1:62,500)' as the earliest topos of its area. Corroborated by Pastmaps and the CSU Long Beach / LA Public Library historical-topo research guides.
findings.counter_evidence: At 1:62,500 these sheets are far too coarse to resolve a dip vat, corral, or bath; they show wetlands, relief and improved roads only, so they neither show nor rule out any working facility. The ScienceBase page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the 1896 date rests on the catalog title plus secondary attestations rather than a directly opened primary page.
findings.citation: USGS HTMC Downey 1896 (ScienceBase 5a8a406be4b00f54eb3ed321, 403 to fetch); Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands Cultural report Appendix G; Pastmaps.com Downey listings; csulb.libguides.com/longbeach/aerial. Grade A2 (map A1, accessed secondhand).

findings.claim: The earliest verified aerial coverage of this landscape is a 1927 USDA frame (UCSB FrameFinder), with a 1928 frame following; this is the standard early-aerial floor for the Los Angeles basin.
findings.supporting: Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands report reproduces a 1927 USDA aerial as Figure D-1 and discusses a 1928 USDA frame (Figure D-2); Fairchild/USDA flew the LA basin in 1927-1928, matching EDR's standard first aerial year for the region.
findings.counter_evidence: 1927 is already ~15 years after the cattle-tick dipping era and ~37 years after this ranch's sheep-dipping era closed; a dip demolished, backfilled, or dismantled before 1927 leaves no aerial signature, and none is reported in the 1927 frame anyway. The 1927 frame verified here images the coastal wetlands margin; frame-level coverage of the inland Bixby-Knolls/Lakewood core in 1927 was not separately confirmed.
findings.citation: Southern Los Cerritos Wetlands Cultural report, Appendix D Figs D-1/D-2 and text; UCSB FrameFinder (library.ucsb.edu/geospatial). Grade A2/B2.

findings.claim: Rancho Los Cerritos was a ~27,000-acre, exceptionally well-watered lowland ranch running up to ~30,000 sheep under Flint, Bixby & Co (1866-1890), making a fixed on-ranch dip facility physically and operationally very plausible.
findings.supporting: Manuel Nieto grant remnant (~27,000 ac); John Temple built the adobe (1844) for cattle; sold 1866 to Flint, Bixby & Co, which converted to sheep; Jotham Bixby resided 1866-1881; ~30,000 sheep sheared twice yearly; strong artesian water (Bouton Lake from an 1895 well) and the LA/San Gabriel River lowlands cross the grant.
findings.counter_evidence: Physical/operational plausibility is not evidence of a located facility or of any residue. The documented vector is sheep-scab dipping (often lime-sulfur or nicotine, not necessarily arsenic), and the dip's location within 27,000 acres -- now dense post-1950 suburbia and channelized river -- is unknown, so plausibility does not narrow to any parcel.
findings.citation: rancholoscerritos.org/about and /about/history; longbeach.gov Rancho Los Cerritos; Wikipedia 'Los Cerritos Ranch House'; hmdb.org marker 50988. Grades B1/B2/C.

findings.claim: California enforced compulsory sheep-scab dipping in this era, and period sheep dips ranged from tobacco/lime-sulfur to arsenical formulations, so the chemistry of the documented Rancho Los Cerritos dip is unknown and not necessarily arsenical or persistent.
findings.supporting: California Statutes of 1900, secs. 597-599c (compulsory dipping of scab-infested sheep), animallaw.info; general dip history: arsenical dips from ~1800, Cooper's arsenic-sulfur dip 1852, alongside tobacco/nicotine and lime-sulfur mixtures widely used for sheep.
findings.counter_evidence: This is statewide regulatory/technical context, not a record of what was mixed at Rancho Los Cerritos. If the ranch used lime-sulfur or nicotine, the arsenic-persistence premise does not apply. No RLC-specific dip formulation was found.
findings.citation: animallaw.info 'California Statutes of 1900: Sections 597-599c'; woolfacts.com sheep-dip history; general BAI/dip literature. Grades A2 (statute) / C (general history).

findings.claim: No dip-vat cleanup or agricultural-arsenic listing tied to the Rancho Los Cerritos footprint was identified in this pass; the soil status of these communities with respect to any ranch-era dip residue remains unstudied.
findings.supporting: No Long Beach/Lakewood/Cerritos/Downey/Bellflower former-ranch dip-vat cleanup site surfaced in searching. DTSC's own Interim Guidance for Sampling Agricultural Properties documents that historical agricultural arsenic/lead is a recognized residential-redevelopment concern, i.e., the hazard class is real and screenable.
findings.counter_evidence: DTSC EnviroStor and State Water Board GeoTracker were NOT exhaustively queried site-by-site for this specific hazard in this run, so absence of a listing is not confirmation of absence; equally, no listing means there is no positive evidence of contamination. The only defensible soil fact remains 'unstudied'.
findings.citation: DTSC EnviroStor (envirostor.dtsc.ca.gov) and DTSC Ag Sampling Guidance (Rev.3, 2008); GeoTracker (geotracker.waterboards.ca.gov). Grade A2 (guidance).

findings.claim: No cattle-tick or sheep-scab dipping record ties a specific dip-vat STRUCTURE (location/coordinates/chemistry) to Rancho Los Cerritos in the newspaper and state-veterinary materials reachable this run.
findings.supporting: The museum attests a dipping practice but no located structure; targeted searches did not return a newspaper or state-veterinarian item fixing a Los Cerritos/Bixby dip-vat to a place.
findings.counter_evidence: This absence largely reflects inaccessible archives, not a search of them: the California Digital Newspaper Collection returned HTTP 403 to automated queries and Chronicling America was not reached this run; the Rancho Los Cerritos museum's own primary collection, the Historical Society of Long Beach, and County Agricultural Commissioner / State Veterinarian tick-and-scab records were not searched. Absence of a located record is not evidence of absence.
findings.citation: WebSearch/WebFetch queries (see dead_ends); Rancho Los Cerritos museum; Historical Society of Long Beach (hslb.org). Grade C (negative-search inference).
